points.title: Why kanji matters
points.explanation: Hiragana and katakana are purely phonetic — each character only represents a sound, with no meaning of its own. Kanji is different: every character carries its own meaning on top of its sound. That's a genuine shift in how reading works. Once you recognize a kanji's meaning, you can often guess roughly what an unfamiliar word means just from the characters it's built from, even before you know how to pronounce it correctly.

examples.japanese: 火山
examples.english: volcano (fire + mountain — the meaning is guessable from the kanji before you even know the reading)

examples.japanese: 人口
examples.english: population (person + mouth — a classic example of guessing meaning from parts)

points.title: Two kinds of readings: 音読み and 訓読み
points.explanation: Most kanji have at least two different pronunciations, called readings, and which one is used depends on the word. 訓読み (kun'yomi) is the native Japanese reading. 音読み (on'yomi) is the reading borrowed from Chinese long ago — if you ever study Mandarin or Cantonese, you'll sometimes notice a family resemblance between a kanji's on'yomi and its Chinese pronunciation, though the two have drifted apart over centuries.

examples.japanese: 山 (やま)
examples.english: mountain — kun'yomi, used when the kanji stands alone

examples.japanese: 富士山 (ふじさん)
examples.english: Mt. Fuji — on'yomi さん, used inside a compound

points.title: A rough guideline for which reading to use
points.explanation: There's no perfect rule, but this heuristic is right most of the time: when a kanji appears mixed together with hiragana in the same word, it's usually read with kun'yomi. When two or more kanji are strung together with no hiragana in between, it's usually read with on'yomi. When a kanji appears completely by itself, kun'yomi is the more common default guess.

examples.japanese: 休む
examples.english: to rest — kanji mixed with hiragana in the same word, read with kun'yomi

examples.japanese: 休日
examples.english: a day off — two kanji strung together with no hiragana, read with on'yomi

examples.japanese: 休み
examples.english: a break, a rest — the kanji's most common standalone form, read with kun'yomi

notes.title: Kanji numbers vs. Arabic numerals
notes.body: Modern Japan mostly uses ordinary Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3...) for everyday numbers — on clocks, signs, license plates — rather than the kanji numeral forms. But the kanji numbers still matter, because they're baked into a large number of fixed words and phrases (dates, counters, set expressions) that you'll need to recognize even though you rarely write a bare number in kanji form yourself.

notes.title: 戻る — to go or come back, return
notes.body: 戻る follows the same [place] に pattern as かえる, but covers more ground: かえる is generally reserved for returning to your actual point of origin (home, most often), while 戻る works for returning to any earlier point — including non-physical ones, like returning to the start of a conversation or a topic.

notes.title: 頑張る — to do your best
notes.body: 頑張る is an extremely common expression in Japanese daily life — said as encouragement to others and as a personal commitment to oneself. The thing you're pushing hard at is marked with を.

notes.title: 泊まる — to stay overnight
notes.body: に marks the place where the overnight stay happens.

notes.title: 働く — to work
notes.body: で marks the place of work — the location where the working happens, following the same event-location logic as で in Book 2.

notes.title: 話す — to speak, to talk
notes.body: 話す has three related but distinct patterns depending on what's being expressed: と marks the person you're talking WITH (a conversation partner); に marks the person you're telling something TO; の...を marks the topic you're talking ABOUT.

points.explanation: As with other counters, the number comes before ページ (page) — 'page five' is 五ページ, not ページ五. Without a particle, ページ acts as a plain counter (a quantity of pages); adding the location particle に turns it into a specific location within a document ('on page five').

points.title: これから vs. いまから
points.explanation: Both mean 'from now' / 'starting now,' referring to something about to happen going forward, and in most contexts they're interchangeable. The one difference: only いまから can be used to describe something in the past relative to a different reference point — a phrase like 'three years ago, from that point' requires いまから, not これから.

notes.title: Combining kanji into 熟語 (compound words)
notes.body: A word made of two or more kanji strung together with no hiragana in between is called 熟語 (jukugo, 'compound word'). When kanji combine this way, the second kanji's reading is often modified by adding a dakuten to its first sound — a word built from 花 (hana, flower) and 火 (hi, fire) doesn't read as 'hanahi,' it reads as 'hanabi' (fireworks), because the combining process shifted the h-sound to a b-sound. This shift is common enough across 熟語 that it's worth checking for it first whenever you're trying to guess an unfamiliar compound's reading.

notes.title: 掛かる — to cost money, to take time
notes.body: 掛かる takes が by default whenever a particle is needed, since amounts of time and money are counters, which never take a particle of their own — the が is marking the surrounding sentence structure, not the amount itself.

notes.title: 買い物（を）する — to shop
notes.body: Shopping (browsing, being out shopping) and buying (actually purchasing a specific item) are different verbs in Japanese and shouldn't be mixed up — 買います describes buying a specific thing, while 買い物します describes the general activity of shopping.

notes.title: 払う — to pay
notes.body: The thing being paid is marked with を. The method of payment (cash, credit card) is marked with で, following the same 'by means of' pattern used elsewhere in this lesson.

points.title: Event frequency with 回

sections.title: Where the planet names come from
sections.body: Most of the Japanese names for the solar system's planets are built from one of these seven elemental kanji plus 星 (star): Mercury is 'water star,' Venus is 'gold star,' Mars is 'fire star,' Jupiter is 'wood star,' and Saturn is 'earth star.' Earth itself is the one exception — rather than using 星, it's written with a different kanji pair meaning 'earth sphere,' since calling Earth a 'star' from Earth's own perspective would be a little strange.

points.title: Introducing the て-form (the command/request form)
points.explanation: This lesson introduces the て-form, used to politely tell or ask someone to do something. Conjugation is based on the final hiragana of a verb's dictionary form, and the pattern only applies to regular verbs — いる/える verbs simply swap their final る for て.

examples.japanese: たべてください。
みて。

points.title: Regular verb て-form endings
points.explanation: Depending on which hiragana a regular verb's dictionary form ends in, that ending changes to a specific て-form pattern: verbs ending in む, ぶ, or ぬ change to んで; verbs ending in う, つ, or る change to って; verbs ending in く change to いて (with 行く/iku as a well-known exception, becoming いって instead); verbs ending in ぐ change to いで; verbs ending in す change to して.

examples.japanese: のむ → のんで
まつ → まって
かく → かいて
いく → いって
はなす → はなして

points.title: The negative て-form ('don't do it')
points.explanation: For the negative command ('don't do X'), regular verbs take their あ-form (the same shift used for the informal negative back in Book 2) and add ないで. いる/える verbs simply drop る and add ないで.

examples.japanese: のまないで。
たべないで。

points.title: Verbs ending in う
points.explanation: Verbs whose dictionary form ends in う shift to わ (not あ) before adding ないで in the negative て-form — the same special-case shift you learned for the informal negative in Book 2, applying consistently here too.

examples.japanese: かわないで。

points.title: Making a request polite with ください
points.explanation: Attaching ください directly after a positive て-form turns a command into a polite request — 'please [verb].' The same particle rules from every other verb form still apply underneath the て-form.

examples.japanese: まどをしめてください。
ここにすわらないでください。

sections.title: Linking the て-form back to the た-form
sections.body: If you already have the た-form (informal past, from Book 2 Lesson 9) memorized for a verb, the て-form is almost free: it follows the exact same conjugation pattern, just swapping た for て at the very end. Anchoring new て-form conjugations to た-forms you already know is a faster way to learn this lesson than memorizing it as a brand new pattern from scratch.

notes.title: Telling 左 and 右 apart by stroke order
notes.body: 左 (left) and 右 (right) look nearly identical, and mixing up their stroke order is a common mistake — one that's actually penalized on formal kanji proficiency tests, not just a cosmetic issue. The distinguishing detail: 右's very first stroke is the downward diagonal stroke, while 左's very first stroke is the horizontal line going across. A simple way to lock this in: right starts by going down, left starts by going across.

notes.title: 思う — to think; 言う — to say, tell
notes.body: Both verbs share the same core pattern: the thought or quote comes first, marked by と, followed by the verb. The quoted or thought material is normally stated in its informal form, even when the overall sentence stays polite — this includes shifting です to だ inside the quoted part.

points.title: The 'quote and thought' marker と
points.explanation: This is a third, unrelated job for と, distinct from 'and' and 'with.' Placed directly after a thought, opinion, or quoted statement, と marks that it's what's being said or thought — the と always comes right after the thought itself, not before it.

examples.japanese: あしたはあめだとおもいます。
examples.romaji: Ashita wa ame da to omoimasu.
examples.english: I think it will rain tomorrow.

points.title: と with 言う (to say)
points.explanation: The same と + informal-quote pattern applies to 言う, used for relaying what someone else said.

examples.japanese: かれはいそがしいといいました。

points.title: と with 聞く (to hear)
points.explanation: The same pattern extends to 聞く when it means 'to hear (that),' as opposed to its other meanings ('to listen' or 'to ask'). から or に can mark who the information came from.

examples.japanese: たなかさんから、けっこんするとききました。
examples.romaji: Tanaka san kara, kekkon suru to kikimashita.
examples.english: I heard from Tanaka that they're getting married.

points.title: When です ends the quoted part
points.explanation: If the material being quoted or thought would normally end in です, that です shifts to its informal form だ before と. Similarly, でした shifts to だった.

examples.japanese: あしたあめだとおもいます。
examples.english: I think it will rain tomorrow. (です shifted to だ before と)

examples.japanese: きのう休みだったといいました。
examples.english: He said it was a day off yesterday. (でした shifted to だった)

points.title: Using adjectives with 思う, 言う, and 聞く
points.explanation: When the quoted material ends in an adjective rather than です, です is simply dropped entirely rather than converted — an adjective on its own already functions as a complete informal statement.

examples.japanese: このりょうりはおいしいとおもいます。
examples.romaji: Kono ryouri wa oishii to omoimasu.
examples.english: I think this dish tastes good.

points.title: Using 何も
points.explanation: 何も always pairs with a negative verb or adjective, meaning 'nothing' or 'not anything.'

examples.japanese: なにもたべませんでした。

points.title: The question word どう
points.explanation: どう means 'how' or 'what,' and is especially common when asking for someone's opinion or impression of something.

examples.japanese: このうたはどうおもいますか。
examples.romaji: Kono uta wa dou omoimasu ka.
examples.english: What do you think of this song?

points.title: Japanese does have a plural — sometimes
points.explanation: Book 1 taught that Japanese nouns don't change between singular and plural, which is mostly true — but attaching たち after certain words does create a real plural, almost always with people (わたしたち, 'we'; あなたたち, 'you all'). It's rarely used with inanimate objects, except when those objects are being given human characteristics.

examples.japanese: わたしたちはがくせいです。
あなたたちはいつきますか。

points.title: たち after a name
points.explanation: When たち follows a specific person's name, it means that person and their associated group — 田中さんたち means 'Tanaka and the people with him,' not 'multiple Tanakas.'

examples.japanese: たなかさんたちはもうかえりました。
examples.romaji: Tanaka san tachi wa mou kaerimashita.
examples.english: Tanaka and the people with him already went home (not 'multiple Tanakas').

sections.title: The kanji behind 'love at first sight'
sections.body: 一目惚れ (hitomebore), the phrase for 'love at first sight,' breaks down surprisingly literally: 一 (one) + 目 (eye) + a form of the verb 惚れる (to fall in love, to be charmed) — 'falling in love within a single glance.' Combine that same 惚れる with 自 (self) instead, and you get 自惚れる (unuboreru), 'to be conceited' — literally 'self love.'

sections.title: How 中 reshapes a word's meaning
sections.body: Adding 中 to certain nouns shifts their meaning to 'in the middle of ___' or 'currently ___-ing' — 勉強 (studying) becomes 勉強中 (in the middle of studying), and 仕事 (work) becomes 仕事中 (on duty, currently working). Watching for this pattern is a quick way to expand your reading vocabulary once you already know the base word.

notes.title: 答える — to answer
notes.body: The same と pattern from Lesson 4 applies here — the answering phrase is marked with と and usually stated in informal form. The thing being answered, and the person being answered, are both marked with に.

examples.japanese: しつもんにこたえました。

points.title: The ています form (ongoing action)
points.explanation: ています is Japanese's equivalent of the English '-ing' form, describing an action that's currently happening or ongoing. It's built by taking a verb's positive て-form and adding います.

examples.japanese: テレビをみています。

points.title: Negating and past-tensing ています
points.explanation: います inside ています conjugates exactly like the standalone verb います always has — shift it to いません for the negative, いました for the past, and いませんでした for the negative past.

examples.japanese: いま、べんきょうしていません。
そのとき、テレビをみていました。
examples.romaji: Sono toki, terebi wo mite imashita.
examples.english: I was watching TV at that time.

examples.japanese: きのう、あめがふっていませんでした。

points.title: ています vs. casual てます
points.explanation: In casual spoken Japanese, the い in ています is very commonly dropped, shortening it to てます. This dropped form is normal and extremely common in speech, but it should generally be avoided in writing.

examples.japanese: なにをしていますか。 ／ なにしてますか。
examples.romaji: Nani wo shite imasu ka. / Nani shitemasu ka.
examples.english: What are you doing? (formal / casual spoken with the い dropped)

points.title: Comparing two things with より and のほうが
points.explanation: This structure states that one thing is more of some quality than another. より attaches to the thing being compared against ('than'); のほうが attaches to the thing that wins the comparison, immediately before the adjective describing it.

examples.japanese: このへやはあのへやよりあかるいです。
examples.romaji: Kono heya wa ano heya yori akarui desu.
examples.english: This room is brighter than that room.

examples.japanese: ちゅうごくりょうりよりにほんりょうりのほうがおいしいです。
examples.romaji: Chuugoku ryouri yori Nihon ryouri no hou ga oishii desu.
examples.english: Japanese food tastes better than Chinese food.

points.title: Using より alone
points.explanation: より can stand on its own without a paired のほうが, meaning 'more than,' 'instead of,' or 'rather than,' depending on context.

examples.japanese: ピザよりすしがたべたいです。
examples.romaji: Piza yori sushi ga tabetai desu.
examples.english: I want to eat sushi rather than pizza.

points.title: Using のほうが alone
points.explanation: のほうが can also stand on its own, without stating what it's being compared against, when the comparison is already clear from context.

examples.japanese: このくるまのほうがいいです。
examples.romaji: Kono kuruma no hou ga ii desu.
examples.english: This car is better (than the other one, from context).

points.title: Saying 'or' with か
points.explanation: か goes between items in a list to mean 'or,' the same structural role と plays for 'and.' Adding か after the very last item in the list is optional.

examples.english: Please write with a pencil or a pen.

sections.title: Kanji hiding on your own body
sections.body: The kanji for numbers one through three (一, 二, 三) are simple enough to trace back to their pictographic origins. Less obviously, the kanji for 'hand' (手) has a rough resemblance to the natural lines visible on the palm of your right hand — not an exact match, but the resemblance is there if you look for it.

sections.title: Telling 'foot' from 'leg'
sections.body: 足 covers both 'foot' and 'leg' in Japanese, which can create genuine ambiguity — 足が痛いです could mean either 'my foot hurts' or 'my leg hurts.' When the distinction matters, 足のうら (literally 'the underside of the foot') specifically means 'sole of the foot,' giving you an unambiguous way to specify foot rather than leg.

sections.title: The Japanese school year
sections.body: Japan's school system is standardized nationwide (unlike the US, where structure can vary by state): 6 years of elementary school, 3 years of junior high, and 3 years of high school. Rather than counting grades continuously from 1st through 12th the way American schools do, Japan restarts the count at the beginning of each level — so 'first year junior high' and 'first year high school' are both real, distinct labels, not a continuation of the elementary numbering.

notes.title: 私立 vs. 市立 — two 'shiritsu's
notes.body: These two words are true homonyms — identical pronunciation, completely different kanji and meaning. 私立 means 'private' (privately run), while 市立 means 'municipal' or 'public.' This ambiguity is real enough that even native speakers sometimes have to clarify which one they mean in conversation, especially when naming a specific school.

notes.title: 会う — to meet
notes.body: The person being met is marked with に for a simple, casual encounter. If the meeting is a planned discussion between the two of you, と is used instead.

notes.title: 遊ぶ — to play
notes.body: The person or thing played with is marked with と. This verb isn't used for playing a sport — する covers that instead.

notes.title: 住む — to live, reside
notes.body: The place lived in is marked with に, not で. Saying you currently live somewhere uses the ています form rather than the plain present tense.

notes.title: 違う — to be wrong, to be different
notes.body: The particle order changes the nuance: [item 1]は[item 2]と違う means 'item 1 is different from item 2,' while [item 1]と[item 2]は違う means 'item 1 and item 2 are different (from each other),' treating both items more as equal partners in the comparison.

notes.title: ホームステイをする — to home stay
notes.body: This specifically describes a foreigner staying with a Japanese host family (or vice versa) — it doesn't apply if host and guest share the same nationality. The location is marked with で.

points.title: Turning い-adjectives into attribute nouns
points.explanation: Dropping the final い from an い-adjective and adding さ turns it into a noun describing that quality as a measurable attribute — comparable to how English turns 'high' into 'height.' Once converted, it behaves like any ordinary noun in a sentence.

points.title: Stringing multiple い-adjectives together
points.explanation: English can simply chain adjectives in a row ('a small, white car'), but Japanese needs every adjective except the very last one in the chain to switch to a special くて form — drop the final い and add くて.

points.title: ています for a resulting state of being
points.explanation: Lesson 5 introduced ています for an action happening right now. It has a second job: describing the resulting state after an action has already occurred — the state you're left in, rather than the action itself as it's happening.

sections.title: A warm-up tongue twister using 生
sections.body: 生 has an unusually large number of readings, which makes it a favorite for Japanese tongue twisters. A well-known one strings together three words that all use 生 read as なま (raw): 生麦、生米、生卵 (namamugi, namagome, namatamago) — 'raw wheat, raw rice, raw eggs.' Try saying it out loud five times quickly; it trips up even native speakers.

points.title: The difference between はじまる and はじめる
points.explanation: These two verbs look and sound almost identical, but they describe fundamentally different situations, and this same intransitive/transitive pairing pattern shows up throughout Japanese, not just with this one verb. はじまる describes something starting on its own, with no specific person causing it — 'the game starts,' with no one named as making it start. はじめる describes someone actively starting something — 'I will start the game,' where a specific person is doing the starting. The clearest test: if your English sentence has an object being acted on by a person ('I started the meeting'), reach for はじめる; if it just describes something happening by itself ('the meeting starts'), reach for はじまる.

notes.title: 吸う — to smoke, to inhale
notes.body: The thing being inhaled or smoked is marked with を. This verb can describe inhaling anything, not only smoking specifically, though smoking is by far its most common everyday meaning.

notes.title: 好きになる / 嫌いになる — to come to like / dislike
notes.body: These describe a change in feeling over time — not liking or disliking something from the start, but growing into that feeling. The thing being grown fond of or averse to is marked with が, except when the verb itself is in て-form, where it switches to を instead.

points.title: Informal questions with なの and の
points.explanation: In casual speech, です in a question can be replaced with なの when the sentence ends in a noun or な-adjective, or simply with の when it ends in a verb or い-adjective. Both carry the same softer, more conversational tone as dropping です altogether while still marking the sentence as a question.

points.title: 以上 and 以下 — over and under an amount
points.explanation: Attaching 以上 after an amount means 'that amount or more'; attaching 以下 means 'that amount or less.' This works with any type of quantity — money, people, objects.

points.title: The たい form ('want to')
points.explanation: Attaching たい to a verb's い-form (regular verbs) or to the dictionary form minus る (いる/える verbs) creates 'want to [verb].' Once in たい form, the verb conjugates exactly like an い-adjective for tense and negation. One important particle shift: the object marker を is usually replaced with が when the verb is in たい form.

examples.japanese: ピザがたべたいです。

examples.english: I want to go to Europe.

points.title: Politeness of the たい form
points.explanation: たい by itself is informal. Adding です after it makes the whole statement polite, without changing たい's own conjugation.

notes.title: たくさん — a lot, many
notes.body: たくさん sits directly in front of a verb to describe doing a lot of something, and works with any verb tense. Attaching の turns it into an adjective that can describe a noun directly.

notes.title: はじめて — the first time
notes.body: はじめて can sit almost anywhere in a sentence to indicate something is being done for the first time, and can also stand completely on its own as はじめてです ('it's the first time'). Attaching の turns it into an adjective as well.

notes.title: だけ — only

points.title: Using とき to say 'when'
points.explanation: とき describes 'when [something happens/happened],' and can attach to a verb, a noun, or an adjective. With a verb, とき always follows the verb's informal dictionary form, and the tense of that verb depends on the actual sequence of events being described, not simply matching the tense of the rest of the sentence.

examples.japanese: わたしがいくとき

points.title: Why verb tense inside とき matters
points.explanation: Whether the verb before とき is present or past tense depends entirely on which event happens first, not on the overall tense of the sentence. 'When my father returns home, we will eat' requires the past tense form of 'return' inside the とき clause (かえったとき) — because the returning has to be complete before the eating starts. Using the present tense form there instead would shift the meaning to something closer to 'at the moment my father leaves to come home.'

examples.japanese: おとうさんがかえったとき、たべます。
examples.english: When my father returns home, we will eat. (return must complete first)

points.title: とき with nouns and い-adjectives

points.title: とき with な-adjectives

points.title: Using な-adjectives
points.explanation: A な-adjective always needs な directly in front of the noun it modifies — の can never substitute for it. Without な, a な-adjective cannot directly modify a noun at all. This is also a good moment to recall that すき and きらい are technically な-adjectives themselves, following this same rule.

points.title: な-adjectives and the 'one' pronoun

points.title: The very useful でしょう
points.explanation: でしょう is genuinely flexible — depending on context and intonation, it can mean 'right?', 'probably,' 'I think,' 'I guess,' or 'I knew you'd say that.' It always sits at the very end of a sentence (or stands completely alone), and any verb before it must be in informal form. Rising intonation tends to push the meaning toward a confirming question ('right?'); flat intonation tends to push it toward a guess or prediction ('probably').

examples.english: You're coming tomorrow, right? (rising) / They'll probably come tomorrow. (flat)

sections.title: Counting years by the emperor's reign
sections.body: Alongside the standard Western calendar year, Japan has a traditional system where years are counted from the start of the current emperor's reign, and each reign is given a specific era name. When this book was written, Japan was in the Heisei era ('everlasting peace'), which ran from 1989 until 2019. Referring to the emperor by his personal name is considered inappropriate — while alive, he's simply called 'the Emperor'; only after his reign ends does he become formally known by his era's name.

notes.title: できる — to be able to do, can do, make
notes.body: The thing that can be done is marked with が (は for emphasis). A very common everyday use is asking whether someone can speak a language, functioning as an alternative to the potential form of 話す.

notes.title: 変わる — to change, turn into
notes.body: The thing changing is marked with が (は for emphasis); what it changes into is marked with に — the same pattern as なる from Lesson 8.

points.title: Sequencing actions with てから
points.explanation: Combining a verb's て-form with から describes doing one action, then another — 'after [doing this], I will [do that].' The tense of the whole sentence is carried by the second action; the て-form verb itself doesn't change for tense.

points.title: Turning い-adjectives into adverbs

notes.title: What are kanji radicals?
notes.body: Many kanji are built by combining smaller, reusable pieces called radicals, and each radical carries its own general meaning — recognizing them lets you take a reasonable guess at an unfamiliar kanji's meaning even before looking it up. For example, さんずい (a compressed, three-stroke form of 水, water) shows up as the left-hand component in water-related kanji like 海 (ocean), 池 (pond), and 汽 (steam). Similarly, くさかんむり (a compressed form of 草, grass) appears at the top of plant-related kanji like 花 (flower) and 茶 (tea). Once you start recognizing a handful of common radicals, previously mysterious kanji start looking a lot more decodable.

sections.title: Endurance as a cultural value
sections.body: 我慢 (gaman) is a genuinely culturally significant word — Japan has a long-associated reputation for valuing quiet emotional restraint and endurance in public settings, and this verb captures that idea directly. It's less about suppressing feeling entirely and more about a particular social norm around not burdening others with visible discomfort.

notes.title: 泳ぐ — to swim
notes.body: で marks the location where the swimming takes place, following the standard event-location pattern.

notes.title: 無くす — to lose (an item)
notes.body: The lost item is marked with を, the standard object-marking pattern.

notes.title: 見つける vs. 見つかる — a transitive/intransitive pair
notes.body: 見つける is transitive — someone finds something, marked with を for the thing found. 見つかる is intransitive — something turns up, without naming who found it, marked with が. This is the same transitive/intransitive pairing as はじめる/はじまる from Lesson 8. (It is not the passive form: the passive of 見つける is 見つけられる.)

notes.title: 我慢する — to endure
notes.body: The thing being endured is marked with を, though this verb is very often used entirely on its own without an explicit object, since the thing being endured is often clear from context.

points.title: Building the potential ('can-do') verb form
points.explanation: The potential form expresses ability — 'can [verb]' or 'can't [verb].' For regular verbs, shift the dictionary form's final う-row hiragana to its え-row counterpart and add る. For いる/える verbs, drop the final る and add られる. A handful of いる/える exception verbs (like かえる, from Book 1) instead follow the regular-verb pattern, consistent with how they've behaved for every other conjugation so far.

examples.japanese: およぐ → およげる
たべる → たべられる
examples.english: to eat -> can eat (いる/える verb)

examples.english: to return -> can return (いる/える exception verb, follows the regular pattern)

points.title: The particle switch for potential verbs
points.explanation: When a verb is in potential form, its object is marked with が instead of を — the same switch you already saw previewed with たい form (Lesson 9) and with できる/話せる earlier in this book. This が-switch is a recurring feature any time a sentence describes ability or desire rather than a directly performed action.

いま、車がかえません。
